item.text: {"text":"The closest match is [Does It Look Sequential? (RecSys 2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.12008), which evaluates sequence shuffling across 15 datasets. Its [official implementation](https://github.com/Antondfger/Does-It-Look-Sequential) keeps trained GRU4Rec models fixed and compares original versus shuffled inference histories using HR@10, NDCG@10 and recommendation-list Jaccard@10. Effects vary sharply: reported GRU4Rec HR@10 changes include −25% on Beauty, −63% on MovieLens-20M and −7% on Yelp. This supports measuring both target accuracy and recommendation stability; weak accuracy changes alone do not establish that predictions are unchanged.\n\nRecency is a related but distinct question. [RSS (2025)](https://eprints.gla.ac.uk/299238/) motivates recency-aware training samples, while [DyS4Rec (2025)](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0893608025000139) addresses historical interactions irrelevant to next-interaction intent. Suggested diagnostic extension: on training-history next-item holdouts, compare equal-sized recent versus older deletions, progressively retain shorter recent suffixes, and shuffle either the whole history or only the prefix while preserving the last item. Keep the trained checkpoint, targets and candidate sets fixed; report paired target-rank changes, HR@10 changes, top-10 Jaccard and final-state cosine distance, with user-level uncertainty. Repack perturbed histories with left padding and read the final nonpadding position. Larger effects from recent deletions indicate recency sensitivity; prefix-shuffle effects with the last item fixed suggest dependence beyond the latest interaction. These are proposed sensitivity probes, not direct measurements of latent intent or causal proof of stale preferences."}
